title: Was there ever a backlash against high-level languages, game engines and pre-made assets? Answered by ChatGPT.
author: Post-reality
selftext:
**Was there ever a backlash against high-level languages, game engines and pre-made assets? Yes.**

And honestly, this is one of the funniest recurring arguments in game development because the *same debate keeps coming back whenever the abstraction level increases.*

Back in the early days, there was absolutely a "serious game programmers work close to the metal" mentality. Assembly wasn't just something enthusiasts used for fun either — it was considered a legitimate competitive advantage because hardware was so constrained and compilers could produce significantly less efficient code.

There are some pretty great examples of this.

In a 1998 *Game Developer Magazine* article, the author describes how game programmers were unusual even at that point in still needing to look at assembly and optimize at the instruction level, while most ordinary software developers had moved to C/C++. The article basically captures the transition from "talk directly to the hardware" to "use higher-level abstractions and optimize where necessary."

And some developers were VERY unapologetic about preferring assembly. Eugene Jarvis, the designer behind games like *Defender* and *Robotron*, explained why Williams/Midway continued using assembly: his argument was essentially that high-level languages sacrificed efficiency for programmer convenience, and that his priority was squeezing the maximum performance out of the hardware.

Chris Sawyer is another famous example. *RollerCoaster Tycoon* was about 99% x86 assembly, with a small amount of C. Sawyer's own explanation was that, on the PCs of the time, a conventional high-level implementation would have forced compromises in simulation complexity or performance.

Then the industry moved further up the abstraction ladder anyway.

By 2007, developers were literally comparing the move from C/C++ to C# with the earlier move from assembly to C/C++. Torpex's developers talked about using C# for the bulk of their game code and dropping back to C/C++ only where they needed tighter performance.

So the pattern is pretty obvious:

**assembly → C → C++ → C# / other high-level languages → scripting → visual scripting**

And at every stage, some developers complained that the new thing was "too abstract", "too slow", "for beginners", etc.

**Game engines went through basically the same cultural argument.**

There has always been a subset of developers who feel that if you're *really* serious, you should write your own engine.

It's not even a new internet phenomenon. AAA studios historically had huge amounts of pride invested in proprietary technology. For example, in a 2009 interview about *Bionic Commando*, GRIN developers talked about their internally developed engine and joked that if they didn't make something in-house, they were "making it in the outhouse."

At the same time, other developers were already making the opposite argument: don't spend your limited resources reinventing the engine when you could spend them making the actual game. In a *Game Developer* interview, Paul Tozour explained that his small studio was simply too small to build its own engine for the game they wanted to make, so they evaluated existing engines specifically so they could concentrate on gameplay.

And that exact argument is **still happening on Reddit**.

You can find r/gamedev threads where people defend making custom engines, people saying "write games, not engines," people arguing that Unity/Unreal are overkill, and people basically saying that building an engine is a separate hobby from building a game.

So yeah, the "using an engine means you're taking shortcuts" mentality absolutely exists. It's just less of one giant historical backlash and more of a recurring subculture.

**Then we got premade assets, and THAT backlash became extremely visible.**

Unity launched its Asset Store in 2010 specifically to let developers buy/share art, code, tools, shaders, animation, etc. to speed up development. By 2014, Unity said the store had more than 15,000 packages and expected over one million users.

And then came the term **"asset flip."**

The important distinction, IMO, is that developers generally weren't angry about the *existence* of premade assets. The anger was directed at people taking store assets, barely changing anything, and trying to sell the result as a finished game.

There are plenty of r/gamedev discussions where developers explicitly make that distinction: using bought assets is normal, especially for solo developers; the problem is when the assets *are essentially the entire product*.

And this became such a significant issue that it wasn't just forum drama. In 2017, Valve removed 173 games associated with Silicon Echo from Steam. Valve said the developer was mass-shipping nearly identical products and abusing Steam's systems; many of the games were associated with the broader "asset flip" phenomenon.

So there was definitely a real backlash around *how* premade assets were being used.

But again, notice the pattern:

**Using somebody else's technology:** bad.

**Using somebody else's engine:** bad.

**Using somebody else's art:** bad.

Then eventually it becomes:

>"Well, obviously nobody expects you to build literally everything yourself."

😂

That's basically where we're at now.

Nobody seriously expects an indie developer to write their own operating system, compiler, renderer, physics engine, animation system, audio middleware, editor, networking stack, model importer, etc. from scratch just to prove they are a "real" developer.

We accepted abstraction because abstraction is how software development scales.

And IMO that's why the current backlash against AI-assisted development feels so familiar. The argument is basically the same old argument wearing a new skin:

**"If the machine/tool did part of the work, did YOU really make the game?"**

We've already had this argument about assembly, C, C++, engines, middleware, asset stores, visual scripting, procedural generation, motion capture, photogrammetry, etc.

The technology changes.

The argument barely does.

**The irony is that the history of game development is basically the history of developers constantly inventing ways to stop doing things manually.**

comments.author: BemaniAK
comments.body:
Asset Flipping is still a problem though tbh, but there is still plenty of legitimate use of premade assets.
I think that's the real crux and AI will be no different, something increases the ability to make stuff, we get 100 new good things that wouldn't have existed otherwise, but that also comes with 10,000 pieces of rubbish that nobody likes.

And that's fine and normal, people screamed about Steam slowly making it easier and easier to publish on their store but it made way for 100 good games and 10,000 bad games, I prefer the 100 good things existing rather than not.

comments.author: whiteseraph12
comments.body:
Some of these points are nonsensical. For example:

\> Resistance to C# and Java: In the early 2000s, the arrival of managed languages with garbage collection was met with significant skepticism from AAA engine developers, who argued that they were “too slow for real games.”

  
Pretty much any relevant engine for making a modern game is written in C/C++. The list of popular games made in Java can be counted on the fingers of two hands, and none of them are AAA or at some technical forefront.

Most of the modern AAA titles are just not possible to make in Java so the argument falls apart.

replies.author: PatchyWhiskers
replies.body: Unity games are scripted in C# but the engine is written in C++.

replies.author: Post-reality
replies.body:
>Most of the modern AAA titles are just not possible to make in Java so the argument falls apart.

AAA titles from 10 years from now won't be possible to be made without AI tools. Productive tools always raise the bar of what's possible to produce.

replies.author: whiteseraph12
replies.body:
Isn't the whole argument in your (I guess your ChatGPT's) point that people resisted new technology historically, and then an example is outlined how game engine developers resisted C# and Java? 

Well which modern engine is built in C# or Java? 90% (if not 99%) of modern AAA games are built in a C/C++ engine and they only might use something like C# (or a custom language) for simple scripting.

replies.author: Post-reality
replies.body: I am not referring AAA games specifically, but the whole industry. C# and Java are common among Mobile and indie gaming scene. Those are just examples.

replies.author: whiteseraph12
replies.body:
Resistance to C# and Java: In the early 2000s, the arrival of managed languages with garbage collection was met with significant skepticism from **AAA** engine developers, who argued that they were “too slow for real games.”

You referred to AAA, and Java/C# are definitely way slower than C/C++. Since your ChatGPT just quoted a general sentiment without any additional reference, it's hard to debate it further. 

I would personally argue though that 'real' games, as in large open worlds or games with many entities and complicated AI are just not feasible to be done in a GC language.

replies.body:

Hold on, what features specifically Java lacks for that? What are those technical and performance requirements that make, say, Cyberpunk 2077 to be un-recreatable in Java?

comments.author: egonosz
comments.body:
So I do not think you made the point here what you wanted to make:  
1. Assembly vs high level

 Many people actually know or check what kind of assembly your code will lead to. If you made accidentally optimisation barriers or if you need to use manual simd. The llms are even more helpful in this.

C# and Java there is really small amount of game engine made in c# or Java and really people do not use them. There is basically zero AAA game based on that type of engine (if we do not count here the original Java). You could get close with c# and tons of unsafe operations, but that is more like porting back c++ into c#.

2. You need the right tools for right job. Depending on what kind of game you want to build will depend what kind of engine you can use. The proprietary engines are not rare at all in game development, they are not dead. The ue and unity are super strong engines, but you cannot do everything with them. This not changed at all. There were backslash against the incoming slop for sure when everyone started to make trash games with unity.

3. No comments on that one, but the asset flips even now get trashed in steam reviews. 

There is lot of nuance with these things, but most of the reasoning behind the backslashes are sound. Even now asset flips and visible generic unity ue visuals get backslash. Many times the backslash is based on perceived effort, behind the game. In my opinion this will get way worse after the LLMs, because the bar will go up.

replies.author: Furbs1337
replies.body: I mean sure, some of the points I can see it. But I definitely had the "made with unity" stigma that it was likely going to be slop or low quality. It took a while of the engine being out and actually playing some good games made with it.

comments.author: GreenBlueStar
comments.body: The higher level languages always get frowned upon by folks used to writing assembly. It's why flash games never really took off and gave rise to publicly Available game engines. The reason is higher level languages abstract a lot of the inner workings of game development and make it harder for a newbie to develop an efficient game. So purists bash tools that do that. AI is probably the ultimate high level language tool where you're basically talking to something that's coding for you. It's natural language at this point and can easily make a very inefficient system if you're not careful. But it's definitely a worthy tool

comments.author: TheReviewerWildTake
comments.body:
Using this as a pro-ai argument leads to a wrong direction, imo...  
  
For example, yes, assembly was popular choice in gamedev for a reason - ppl who knew how to work with it, were slaying with performance and compact size, and have achieved mind-blowing results with it, which was appreciated by users without newest computers.   
  
They were not rejecting tech out of weird ideological viewpoints. They had a strong point about trade-offs that everyone knew were true.  
Tech and programming moved on because hardware got significantly better. 

Basically, we should not conflate ideology with sane opinions, that made sense in a specific time, for specific type of customer etc. 

I don\`t mind people who are saying that lots of AI games are actually bad.  
It is reality.   
  
On the other hand, I can\`t agree with people who start witch-hunts due to devs having AI in a clearly well made product, or with people who pretend that everything with AI is by definition a slop, when it is basically NOT a reality.

Asset flip also was legit annoying, because tons of scammers have used it to drain money from naive kick-starters, who were presented with vertical slices\\renders of fake games, that looked like real games.  
But again - there is no comparison of someone who disliked that, with a person who enjoys a game up until he discovers AI disclosure, and suddenly decides to virtue signal...
